facts.text: The applicants were born in 1973 and 1978 respectively and are currently being held in the Gaziosmanpaşa Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre in Kırklareli.

anchor.surface_text: 6.  The applicants were born in 1973 and 1978 respectively and are currently being held in the Gaziosmanpaşa Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre in Kırklareli.

facts.text: The applicants joined the People’s Mojahedin Organisation in Iran (PMOI) in 1992 and 2001 respectively and lived in Al-Ashraf camp in Iraq until they left the organisation in 2005 and 2006 respectively.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  The applicants joined the People’s Mojahedin Organisation in Iran (“the PMOI”, also known as the “Mojahedin-e-Khalq Organization”) in 1992 and 2001 respectively. They arrived in Iraq on unspecified dates. They lived in Al-Ashraf camp, where PMOI members were accommodated in Iraq, until they left the organisation in 2005 and 2006 respectively, because they disagreed with the PMOI’s goals and methods.

facts.text: After leaving the PMOI, the applicants went to the Temporary Interview and Protection Facility (TIPF), a camp created by the United States forces in Iraq, later named Ashraf Refugee Camp (ARC).

anchor.surface_text: After leaving the PMOI, they went to the Temporary Interview and Protection Facility (“TIPF”), a camp created by the United States forces in Iraq. This facility was subsequently named the Ashraf Refugee Camp (“ARC”).

facts.text: On 5 May 2006 and 16 October 2007, the applicants were recognised as refugees by the UNHCR Headquarters in Geneva during their stay in Iraq.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  On 5 May 2006 and 16 October 2007, after being interviewed, the applicants were recognised as refugees by the UNHCR Headquarters in Geneva during their stay in Iraq.

facts.text: The UNHCR found the first applicant had a well-founded fear of persecution in Iran on grounds of political opinion and his link to the PMOI for 10 years.

anchor.surface_text: As regards the first applicant, the UNHCR found that he had a well-founded fear of persecution in Iran on grounds of his political opinion, his character and the firm conviction with which he held his political opinions. In particular, having regard to the applicant’s link to the PMOI for 10 years, to the treatment of members of the PMOI in Iran and to his explicit opinions on the need for a secular State in his country of origin, the UNHCR considered that the applicant had established to a reasonable degree that his situation would be followed up by the security agencies which would make his stay in Iran intolerable if he returned there.

facts.text: The UNHCR found the second applicant had a well-founded fear of violations by Iranian authorities including arbitrary deprivation of life, torture, ill-treatment, arbitrary arrest or detention, and unfair trial.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  As regards the second applicant, the UNHCR found that he had a well-founded fear of violations by Iranian authorities of, inter alia, his right to life through an arbitrary or unlawful deprivation of life, freedom from torture, ill-treatment, arbitrary arrest or detention, as well as his right to a fair and public trial.

facts.text: In April 2008 the TIPF was closed down and the applicants, along with other former PMOI members, were transferred to northern Iraq.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  In April 2008 the TIPF was closed down and the applicants, along with other former PMOI members, were transferred to northern Iraq.

facts.text: The applicants arrived in Turkey on an unspecified date, were arrested by security forces, and deported back to Iraq on 17 June 2008 for illegal entry.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On an unspecified date the applicants arrived in Turkey. They were arrested by security forces and, as they had entered Turkish territory illegally, were deported back to Iraq on 17 June 2008.

facts.text: The applicants immediately re-entered Turkey after their deportation to Iraq on 17 June 2008.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  They immediately re-entered Turkey.

facts.text: On 21 June 2008 the applicants were arrested by gendarmerie officers at a road checkpoint in Muş due to false passports.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  On 21 June 2008 they were arrested by road checkpoint gendarmerie officers from the Gökyazı gendarme station, in Muş, as their passports were found to be false.

facts.text: On 21 June 2008 the applicants stated to gendarmerie officers that they would be executed if returned to Iran and wished to go to Istanbul to request asylum and leave for Canada.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  On 21 June 2008 the applicants made statements to the gendarmerie officers. The applicants contended that they would be executed if returned to Iran, due to their opposition to the Iranian Government’s policies, and that their lives had also been at risk in Iraq. They stated that they wished to go to Istanbul in order to request asylum and leave for Canada.

facts.text: The applicants were placed in the foreigners’ department at the police headquarters in the Hasköy district of Muş after their arrest.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  The applicants were subsequently placed in the foreigners’ department at the police headquarters in the Hasköy district of Muş.

facts.text: On 23 June 2008 the Muş public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment charging the applicants with illegal entry into Turkey.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  On 23 June 2008 the Muş public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Muş Magistrates’ Court, charging the applicants with illegal entry into Turkey.

facts.text: On 23 June 2008 the applicants were brought before the Muş Magistrates’ Court, convicted of illegal entry but sentence deferred for five years.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  On the same day the applicants were brought before the Muş Magistrates’ Court. Noting that the applicants would be deported, the judge communicated the bill of indictment to the applicants and took their statements regarding the charge against them. The applicants submitted that they had left Iran as they faced a risk of death in that country and that they had come to Turkey illegally, with the assistance of a smuggler, in order to go to Canada where they had family. The magistrates’ court convicted the applicants as charged but decided to defer the imposition of a sentence for a period of five years in accordance with Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts.text: According to the applicants, on 28 June 2008 the authorities attempted to deport them to Iran but the deportation was prevented by the applicants pretending not to understand Farsi.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  According to the applicants’ submissions, on 28 June 2008 the national authorities once again attempted to deport them, this time to Iran. The applicants prevented their deportation by speaking Arabic and pretending not to understand Farsi. Consequently, the Iranian authorities refused to admit them to Iran.

facts.text: On 30 June 2008 the director of the Muş branch of the Human Rights Association visited the applicants at police headquarters and reported the first applicant had attempted suicide after being told he would be deported to Iran.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  On 30 June 2008 the director of the Muş branch of the Human Rights Association, Mr Vedat Şengül, went to the Hasköy police headquarters to visit the applicants at the request of the UNHCR Ankara office. According to Mr Şengül’s submissions, on the day of his visit the first applicant had attempted to commit suicide as he had been told by a police officer that he would be deported to Iran.

facts.text: On 30 June and 1 and 2 July 2008 the applicants made further statements to the police, confirming their former PMOI membership and that they came to Turkey to apply to UNHCR.

anchor.surface_text: 20.  On 30 June and 1 and 2 July 2008 the applicants made further statements to the police and contended that they were former members of the PMOI. The first applicant noted that he had had English, Farsi and Arabic lessons as well as military training when he was in the organisation. He also stated that, while in the TIPF, he had been a photographer and taught Arabic. He said that he had not been involved in any armed activity. The second applicant stated that, apart from the aforementioned languages, he had also learned Turkish when he had been a member of the PMOI. He contended that he had lived in the TIPF for two years and had never been involved in any armed activity. Both applicants stated that they had come to Turkey in order to apply to the UNHCR, following advice by AmericanUSA officials to do so.

facts.text: The applicants submitted identical petitions in Farsi to the police in Hasköy requesting temporary stay in Turkey to process their resettlement cases with UNHCR.

anchor.surface_text: 21.  The applicants submitted identical petitions in Farsi to the police in Hasköy, which read as follows: “We entered Turkey with the assistance of a smuggler from the city of Diyana. We are refugees and used to reside in Erbil, Iraq. We came to Turkey in order to contact the UNHCR and ask it to process our [resettlement] cases. The UNHCR’s headquarters in Iraq was blown up by terrorists and it no longer has an office there. We request to stay in Turkey temporarily so that our cases can be processed. Our friends advised us that the only way to contact the UNHCR was to come to Turkey. We need a lawyer before we communicate [with you] further.”

facts.text: The applicants were held at the Hasköy police headquarters until 26 September 2008, when they were transferred to the Kırklareli Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre.

anchor.surface_text: 23.  The applicants were held at the Hasköy police headquarters, in Muş until 26 September 2008, when they were transferred to the Kırklareli Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre.

facts.text: On 18 October 2008 the applicants drafted petitions to the Kırklareli governor’s office seeking temporary asylum in Turkey but had not received any reply.

anchor.surface_text: 24.  On 18 October 2008 the applicants drafted petitions addressed to the Kırklareli governor’s office and sought temporary asylum in Turkey. According to the information in the case file, the applicants have not yet received any reply to their petitions.

facts.text: On 15 December 2008 the second applicant married another Iranian asylum seeker held in the Kırklareli Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre.

anchor.surface_text: 25.  On 15 December 2008 the second applicant married another Iranian asylum seeker held in the Kırklareli Foreigners’ Admission and Accommodation Centre. The director of the Centre assisted them in obtaining their marriage certificate.

facts.text: On 16 January 2009 the second applicant had a power of attorney notarised for lawyers in Istanbul to represent him in Turkey.

anchor.surface_text: 26.  On 16 January 2009 the second applicant had a power of attorney notarised for Mr A. Baba, and subsequently Ms S. Uludağ, lawyers practising in Istanbul, to represent him in Turkey. The notary agreed to notarise the power of attorney on the basis of the aforementioned marriage certificate.

facts.text: On 16 March 2009 the second applicant’s lawyer filed a petition with the Ministry of the Interior challenging the second applicant’s detention but no reply was received.

anchor.surface_text: 27.  On 16 March 2009 the second applicant’s lawyer filed a petition with the Ministry of the Interior, challenging the second applicant’s detention. According to the information in the case file, the second applicant has not yet received any reply to his petition.

facts.text: On 25 March 2009, upon a request from the UNHCR, the Government of Sweden agreed to examine the applicants’ cases for resettlement, which was still pending.

anchor.surface_text: 28.  On 25 March 2009, upon a request from the UNHCR, the Government of Sweden agreed to examine the applicants’ cases for resettlement there. According to the information in the case file, that examination is still pending.

precedents.cited_holding: Lodging an application does not automatically suspend deportation; specific stay order needed.

anchor.surface_text: The right to political asylum is not explicitly protected by either the Convention or its Protocols (see Salah Sheekh v. the Netherlands, no. 1948/04, § 135, ECHR 2007‑I). However, expulsion by a Contracting State may give rise to an issue under Article 3, and hence engage the responsibility of that State under the Convention, where substantial grounds have been shown for believing that the individual concerned, if deported, faces a real risk of being subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3.

precedents.cited_proposition: Political asylum is not explicitly protected but expulsion may engage Article 3 if real risk exists.
precedents.cited_holding: Expulsion may violate Article 3 if real risk of ill-treatment exists.

anchor.surface_text: Article 3 implies an obligation not to deport the person in question to that country (see Saadi v. Italy [GC], no. 37201/06, § 125, 28 February 2008).

precedents.cited_proposition: Article 3 implies an obligation not to deport where real risk of ill-treatment exists.
precedents.cited_holding: States must not deport persons to countries where they face real risk of ill-treatment.

precedents.citation: Mamatkulov and Askarov v. Turkey [GC], nos. 46827/99 and 46951/99, § 67, ECHR 2005‑I

anchor.surface_text: The assessment whether there are substantial grounds for believing that the applicant faces such a real risk inevitably requires that the Court assess the conditions in the receiving country against the standards of Article 3 of the Convention (see Mamatkulov and Askarov v. Turkey [GC], nos. 46827/99 and 46951/99, § 67, ECHR 2005‑I). These standards imply that the ill-treatment the applicant alleges he will face if returned must attain a minimum level of severity if it is to fall within the scope of Article 3.

precedents.cited_proposition: Court must assess receiving country's conditions against Article 3 standards for real risk.
precedents.cited_holding: Ill-treatment must reach minimum severity to engage Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: These standards imply that the ill-treatment the applicant alleges he will face if returned must attain a minimum level of severity if it is to fall within the scope of Article 3. The assessment of this is relative, depending on all the circumstances of the case (see Hilal v. the United Kingdom, no. 45276/99, § 60, ECHR 2001‑II).

precedents.cited_proposition: Ill-treatment must attain minimum severity to fall within Article 3 scope.
precedents.cited_holding: Assessment of severity is relative to circumstances.

anchor.surface_text: Article 3 may thus also apply in situations where the danger emanates from persons or groups of persons who are not public officials. What is relevant in this context is whether an applicant is able to obtain protection against and seek redress for the acts perpetrated against him or her (see Salah Sheekh, cited above, § 147).

precedents.cited_proposition: Article 3 applies even if danger comes from non-state actors if no protection is available.
precedents.cited_holding: Relevant is whether applicant can obtain protection or redress.

anchor.surface_text: In cases where an applicant alleges that he or she is a member of a group systematically exposed to a practice of ill-treatment, the protection of Article 3 of the Convention enters into play when the applicant establishes that there are serious reasons to believe the existence of that practice and his or her membership of the group concerned (see Saadi, cited above, § 132).

precedents.cited_proposition: Article 3 protection applies when group is systematically ill-treated and applicant is member.
precedents.cited_holding: No need for further special features if protection would be illusory.

anchor.surface_text: This will be determined in the light of the applicant’s account and the information on the situation in the country of destination in respect of the group in question (see Salah Sheekh, cited above, § 148).

precedents.cited_proposition: Assessment based on applicant's account and country situation regarding group.
precedents.cited_holding: Protection under Article 3 depends on credible evidence of group risk.

anchor.surface_text: The Court is not precluded, however, from having regard to information which comes to light subsequent to the extradition or deportation (see Mamatkulov and Askarov, cited above, § 69).

precedents.cited_proposition: Court may consider information arising after deportation in assessing risk.
precedents.cited_holding: Subsequent information relevant to risk assessment.

anchor.surface_text: The Government have not put forward any argument or document capable of dispelling doubts about the applicants’ allegations concerning the risks they might face in Iran and Iraq (see Saadi, cited above, §§ 128 and 129).

precedents.cited_proposition: Government must dispel doubts about risk to avoid violation of Article 3.
precedents.cited_holding: Lack of evidence from Government supports finding of real risk.

anchor.surface_text: The indirect removal of an alien to an intermediary country does not affect the responsibility of the expelling Contracting State to ensure that he or she is not, as a result of its decision to expel, exposed to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention (see T.I. v. the United Kingdom (dec.), no. 43844/98, ECHR 2000-III; Salah Sheekh, cited above, § 141).

precedents.cited_proposition: Expelling State remains responsible for indirect removal exposing to Article 3 risk.
precedents.cited_holding: Indirect removal does not absolve responsibility under Article 3.
